title: CASE R-14 — the paper house
intro: Field Recovery reopened the file on the houses that were taken by paper. Not by fire or flood: by forms. A loan the government alleged was priced and steered by race, two generations after the 1937 map graded this city. Sworn statements signed by the stack. A defense that asked for one sheet of paper, and court rules that will take a sworn copy in its place. A city sale for a family's unpaid bills. And some of the people in the offices sworn to stand between the block and the machine, keeping false books of their own. Six instruments, every one in print. Read them in order; each reading opens the next. Every instrument in this file is paper. None of them is a place, and there is no house to go to. The file will not tell you that you can win. It will only show you how the machine works.

stations.title: i · the referral
stations.clue: Two generations after the red line kept the money out, the money came back, and the government alleged it came back priced by race. In 2012 the Justice Department settled with the country's largest home mortgage originator over claims that Black and Hispanic borrowers who qualified for better loans were charged more or put into subprime ones. The bank denied it, and no court ruled on it. Case D-8 read this release for its figure; read it again for a name. The Department was not the only office looking: find the federal regulator that ran its own parallel investigation of the bank's lending in the Baltimore and Washington metro areas, then referred what it found.

link.label: U.S. Department of Justice — the 2012 fair lending settlement (archived copy)

stations.prompt: one word: the official the regulator is named for (the first word of the title, not its initials)

stations.title: ii · the stamps
stations.clue: In the autumn of 2010 the country learned that foreclosure paper had been signed by the stack, and some of it stamped by notaries alleged to have notarized without watching anyone sign. Maryland went after the stamps. A trade paper reported what the Maryland Secretary of State did to the notaries it found, and in which months. The headline gives the total. Read past it: how many lost their commissions in August?

link.label: HousingWire — Maryland's notaries and the foreclosure probe (October 2010)

stations.prompt: digits only: how many notaries were removed in August

stations.title: iii · the note
stations.clue: Some homeowners answered with four words: show me the note. The original promise to pay, signed at the closing table, had passed from lender to lender, and some attorneys, quoted in a 2009 news report the encyclopedia cites, estimated that the papers behind as many as half the mortgages made from 2001 through 2008 were lost or destroyed. Read the encyclopedia's section on that defense (on a phone, tap its heading to open it). It names, in a single word, the question the whole strategy rests on: who has the legal right to sue.

link.label: Wikipedia — the produce-the-note defense (the version checked for this case)

stations.prompt: one word: the question of who may sue

stations.title: iv · the sale
stations.clue: The city has a sale of its own. Each year it sells the unpaid city bills on homes to outside bidders, and the bidders then charge the owner interest and fees, as state law allows. The city's housing department publishes the line a home must cross before it can be put up for that sale. Open its tax sale page and read the figure for a home its owner lives in.

link.label: Baltimore City housing department — tax sale prevention

stations.prompt: digits only, no cents: the dollar line for an owner-occupied home

stations.title: v · the badge
stations.clue: Some of the people sworn to protect the block were robbing it. Members of a specialized unit of the city's police department, named for tracing guns, robbed people they stopped and wrote false reports to hide it. Read the U.S. Attorney's release on one detective's sentencing. Besides the robberies, he admitted cheating the city on his timesheets. Find the kind of pay he claimed for hours he did not work.

link.label: U.S. Attorney, District of Maryland — a detective's sentencing (archived copy)

stations.prompt: one word: the kind of pay he faked

stations.title: vi · the books
stations.clue: In 2020 a former mayor of Baltimore was sentenced to three years in federal prison. She had sold the University of Maryland Medical System tens of thousands of her own children's books, kept some of the books it paid for, and sold copies to other buyers who did not know. The U.S. Attorney's release describes how the money was disguised: a contract, a business ledger, and fake invoices made at her urging. Find the one word the release uses for what was done to the dates on those invoices.

link.label: U.S. Attorney, District of Maryland — the former mayor's sentencing (archived copy)

stations.prompt: one word: what was done to the dates on the invoices
